Explanation: These four specialized cutaneous low-threshold mechanoreceptors encode distinct tactile features: Meissner corpuscles (flutter, ~5-50 Hz), Pacinian corpuscles (high-frequency vibration), Merkel discs (sustained pressure and fine texture; slowly adapting type I), and Ruffini endings (skin stretch; slowly adapting type II).
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Skin touch receptors; Cutaneous tactile mechanoreceptors
Notes: Title corrected: 'Encapsulated or specialized' was inaccurate because Merkel discs are UNENCAPSULATED epidermal Merkel cell-neurite complexes, whereas Meissner, Pacinian, and Ruffini are corpuscular/encapsulated. Do not attribute proprioception to Merkel or low-frequency vibration to Ruffini. Added-reference verification: Crawford & Caterina, Toxicol Pathol 2020; Del Valle et al., Microsc Res Tech 2012; Abad et al., Nat Commun 2024.

Explanation: A corticospinal (upper motor neuron) lesion can produce increased deep tendon reflexes, velocity-dependent spasticity, increased tone, and a Babinski (extensor plantar) response.
Source Section: Descending Spinal Cord Tracts; Ischemic Cerebrovascular Accidents; PDF pp. 25, 157
Notes: Spasticity is a velocity-dependent subtype of hypertonia, so tiles 2 and 3 partially overlap; retain as distinct exam concepts but flag redundancy when building a 16-tile board. Acute UMN lesions may be initially flaccid (spinal shock); these signs are characteristic, not obligatory immediately after injury.

Explanation: Loss of lower motor neuron input can produce muscle wasting, fasciculations, reduced or absent reflexes, and low tone.
Source Section: Descending Spinal Cord Tracts; Invasive Spinal Cord Disease; PDF pp. 25, 64
Notes: Localize specifically to lower motor neuron (anterior horn cell, root, peripheral nerve) dysfunction; not every peripheral neuromuscular disorder produces all four. Board overlap: fasciculations and atrophy also appear in ALS (mixed UMN/LMN) categories.

Explanation: These descending brainstem motor pathways influence posture, tone, orienting movements, and balance outside the corticospinal (pyramidal) system.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Brainstem descending motor pathways; Non-pyramidal descending tracts
Source Section: Descending Spinal Cord Tracts; PDF pp. 28
Notes: Clean canonical set of the four classic extrapyramidal descending tracts. No competing category of equal strength.

Connection Title: Cranial nerves with medially located somatic motor nuclei
Explanation: The general somatic efferent nuclei of CN III, IV, VI, and XII lie near the brainstem midline, a useful medial-localization pattern.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Medial (GSE) brainstem motor cranial nerves; Pure somatic motor cranial nerves
Source Section: Brainstem Anatomy; Cranial Nerves; PDF pp. 37, 98, 100, 102, 112
Notes: Also fits the broader 'pure somatic motor cranial nerves' category (the GSE group III/IV/VI/XII) - same four, treated as an accepted synonymous framing rather than a competing category. Use nucleus location (medial), not peripheral nerve course. Verified: Sarma et al., Pediatr Radiol 2021 (medial motor / lateral sensory rule).

Explanation: These motor and sensory structures form the classic 'medial brainstem' localization framework (the 4 M's).
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Medial brainstem structures; The four M's
Notes: Do NOT reproduce the source claim that the MLF does not enter the medulla; the MLF extends throughout the brainstem. Tile 4 is a collective category (nuclei), and this set overlaps NEU-005; keep them off the same board. Verified against standard medial/lateral brainstem rule (Sarma et al., Pediatr Radiol 2021).

Explanation: Lateral brainstem lesions can disrupt body pain-temperature, ipsilateral facial pain-temperature, sympathetic, and cerebellar pathways (the lateral 'side' structures).
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Lateral brainstem localization pathways; The four S's
Source Section: Brainstem Anatomy; Ischemic Cerebrovascular Accidents; PDF pp. 37, 162
Notes: Spinal trigeminal nucleus is the pain-temperature component of the broader trigeminal sensory nuclear complex. Spinocerebellar pathways are a collective tile. Overlaps Wallenberg (NEU-036); keep off the same board.

Connection Title: Functional regions of the frontal lobe
Explanation: These frontal regions govern voluntary movement, executive behavior, conjugate gaze, and speech production respectively.
Notes: Broca area refers to the language-dominant hemisphere. Clean localization set.

Tile 4: Ipsilateral LMN signs at the lesion level
Explanation: Spinal cord hemisection affects the ipsilateral corticospinal tract and dorsal column, the crossing spinothalamic (pain-temperature) pathway, and lower motor neurons at the injured segment.
Source Section: Ascending Spinal Cord Tracts; Descending Spinal Cord Tracts; Spinal Cord Syndromes; PDF pp. 19, 26, 58
Notes: Contralateral pain-temperature loss typically begins approximately 1-2 segments below the lesion. Segmental LMN signs depend on anterior horn/root involvement at the level. Classic, well-defined localization set.

Explanation: Tetanospasmin blocks inhibitory neurotransmitter release, producing sustained or stimulus-triggered spasms including jaw locking (trismus), a grimacing facial contraction (risus sardonicus), and back arching (opisthotonus).
Source Section: Invasive Spinal Cord Disease; PDF pp. 62
Notes: 'Spastic muscle spasms' here denote toxin-mediated spasms from loss of inhibition, not a primary corticospinal UMN syndrome; wording reflects that.

Explanation: Inflammatory CNS demyelination can cause optic nerve dysfunction, MLF-related internuclear gaze dysfunction, heat-related worsening (Uhthoff), and an electric sensation on neck flexion (Lhermitte).
Notes: None is individually specific to MS; bilateral INO in a young patient is particularly suggestive. Do not treat INO as a peripheral CN III palsy (it is an MLF lesion). Lhermitte/Uhthoff also occur in other myelopathies.

Explanation: MRI can reveal periventricular demyelinating lesions (including the perivenular 'Dawson fingers' pattern), while CSF may show intrathecal oligoclonal bands and mild lymphocytic inflammation.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: MRI and CSF findings in MS
Notes: Dawson fingers are a specific periventricular lesion pattern, so tiles 1 and 2 partially overlap. Pleocytosis should be mild (typically <50 cells/uL); a markedly elevated count suggests an alternative diagnosis.

Explanation: PML results from JC-virus-mediated oligodendrocyte injury in immunosuppressed hosts and classically produces nonenhancing white matter lesions; natalizumab is a recognized risk exposure.
Notes: Not every exposed patient develops PML. Contrast enhancement can occur, particularly with immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS); nonenhancement is typical rather than universal.

Explanation: Ionotropic GABA-A and glycine receptors are ligand-gated chloride channels mediating inhibition; benzodiazepines and barbiturates are positive allosteric modulators that enhance GABA-A chloride conductance.
Notes: GABA tile qualified to GABA-A, because GABA also acts at metabotropic GABA-B receptors (not a chloride channel). Benzodiazepines/barbiturates are allosteric modulators, not direct equivalent agonists. Mixed neurotransmitter/drug tiles are intentional for the shared-effect category.

Explanation: These agents reversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase, increasing synaptic acetylcholine; their CNS vs peripheral sites of action and clinical uses differ.
Notes: Not an exhaustive class; organophosphates/echothiophate are irreversible and excluded. BOARD OVERLAP: donepezil also appears in NEU-051; do not place both connections on the same 16-tile board, and avoid pairing with rivastigmine/galantamine.

Connection Title: Ocular and bulbar myasthenia gravis symptoms
Explanation: Fatigable weakness of extraocular, eyelid, and bulbar muscles produces these symptoms in myasthenia gravis, typically with preserved pupillary function.
Notes: These oculobulbar symptoms also occur in botulism, LEMS, and other neuromuscular disorders. Explanation should retain fatigability and pupil sparing. Avoid competing oculobulbar categories (botulism) on the same board.

Explanation: LEMS impairs presynaptic acetylcholine release via P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium-channel autoimmunity; brief exercise transiently facilitates strength and reflexes, and roughly half of cases are paraneoplastic (most often SCLC).
Notes: SCLC is present in ~50-60% of cases (association, not required for diagnosis). Facilitation is with brief/short exercise, not sustained exertion. Verified: El-Wahsh & Reddel, Int Rev Neurobiol 2025; Punga et al., Lancet Neurol 2022; Maddison et al., Sci Rep 2020.

Explanation: A complete oculomotor palsy impairs eyelid elevation and most extraocular muscles; parasympathetic involvement produces mydriasis and a 'down-and-out' eye.
Notes: Pupillary dilation depends on parasympathetic fiber involvement; ischemic (e.g., diabetic) palsies classically spare the pupil. This set is specifically a complete, pupil-involving palsy (e.g., compressive/PCom aneurysm).

Connection Title: Structures passing through the superior orbital fissure
Explanation: CN III, IV, VI, and the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve all enter the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Nerves traversing the superior orbital fissure; Cavernous sinus-related nerves
Notes: All four also traverse/are affected by the cavernous sinus - an accepted related framing, not a distinct competing category. Do NOT add V2 (exits via foramen rotundum). CN VI entry via SOF confirmed by standard anatomy.

Connection Title: Branch-dependent effects of proximal facial nerve injury
Tile 2: Loss of anterior two-thirds tongue taste
Explanation: A sufficiently proximal facial nerve lesion can affect facial expression, chorda tympani taste, the stapedius (hyperacusis), and parasympathetic (greater petrosal) lacrimal output.
Notes: All four require a lesion proximal to the relevant branch points (at/above the geniculate region). A distal parotid-region motor lesion does not explain taste, lacrimation, or stapedius deficits. Verified: Gilden, NEJM 2004; ACR Appropriateness Criteria Cranial Neuropathy 2022.

Tile 1: Loss of posterior one-third tongue taste
Tile 3: Impaired afferent limb of gag reflex
Explanation: CN IX injury impairs posterior tongue taste/sensation, pharyngeal sensation, the sensory (afferent) limb of the gag reflex, and its only motor target, the stylopharyngeus.
Notes: Dysphagia from isolated stylopharyngeus weakness is usually minor. Clean, specific CN IX set.

Tile 4: Uvula deviates away from the lesion
Explanation: Vagal motor dysfunction weakens the palate, pharynx, and larynx, impairing voice and swallowing and causing asymmetric palatal elevation (uvula points away from the lesioned side).
Notes: A lesion must involve the relevant branches; isolated recurrent laryngeal nerve injury causes hoarseness without palatal/gag findings.

Connection Title: Retrochiasmal sites causing homonymous visual field loss
Explanation: Unilateral lesions posterior to the optic chiasm disrupt corresponding portions of the contralateral visual field in both eyes (homonymous defects).
Notes: Pattern varies by site/extent: partial radiation lesions cause quadrantanopia (temporal=superior/Meyer loop; parietal=inferior). Macular sparing is possible, not obligatory, with occipital infarction.

Explanation: These conditions impair external- or middle-ear sound transmission rather than primarily damaging cochlear sensory transduction.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: External and middle ear causes of hearing loss
Notes: Ambiguity raised to 1: tile 4 (obstructing canal mass, e.g., exostosis/tumor/foreign body) must be read as non-cerumen to remain distinct from tile 1; otherwise tiles 1 and 4 are near-duplicates. Flag this overlap on a board.

Explanation: These conditions damage cochlear sensory function or the vestibulocochlear nerve, producing sensorineural hearing impairment.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Cochlear or CN VIII hearing loss
Notes: Not an exhaustive class. Frequency pattern differs: Meniere affects low frequencies early; presbycusis and noise injury affect high frequencies. Vestibular schwannoma SNHL is typically asymmetric/unilateral.

Explanation: These disorders affect the peripheral vestibular apparatus or CN VIII and can produce vertigo with differing timing and hearing features.
Notes: Vestibular schwannoma more often causes slowly progressive imbalance/asymmetric hearing loss than acute spinning vertigo; vertigo is possible, not universal. Keep lower priority than tighter mechanism-based groups; central vertigo is the key contrast category.

Explanation: Displaced otoconia (canaliths) cause brief positional vertigo; posterior-canal BPPV is diagnosed with the Dix-Hallpike maneuver and treated with the Epley canalith-repositioning maneuver.
Notes: Dix-Hallpike and Epley apply primarily to posterior-canal BPPV; horizontal-canal variants require the supine roll test and different repositioning (e.g., BBQ roll). Title/scope narrowed to posterior canal for accuracy.

Explanation: Medulloblastoma is an aggressive embryonal cerebellar tumor that may show primitive small round blue cells and Homer-Wright rosettes and disseminate through the CSF.
Notes: Do not require a vermian location for every molecular subgroup (WNT/SHH/group 3/group 4 differ in site). Homer-Wright rosettes are characteristic but not unique (also neuroblastoma).

Explanation: Pilocytic astrocytoma is a low-grade (WHO grade 1) astrocytic tumor, often cystic and cerebellar in children, with GFAP expression and characteristic Rosenthal fibers.
Notes: GFAP positivity and Rosenthal fibers are not individually specific; cystic architecture and cerebellar location are typical but not universal (optic pathway/brainstem sites occur). Combined clues define it.

Explanation: Childhood adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma is a suprasellar epithelial tumor derived from Rathke pouch remnants, with keratinizing ('wet keratin') and often calcified cystic ('motor-oil' cyst) pathology.
Notes: Wet keratin and calcification are specific to the adamantinomatous subtype; do not apply to adult papillary craniopharyngioma (BRAF V600E, non-calcified).

Explanation: Glioblastoma (WHO grade 4) shows necrosis bordered by palisading tumor cells and abnormal microvascular proliferation; some cross the corpus callosum, and many harbor EGFR alterations.
Source Section: Adult Primary Brain Tumors; PDF pp. 149
Notes: EGFR alteration and butterfly configuration are characteristic, not universal. EGFR amplification and overexpression are related but distinct molecular statements; tile wording kept general.

Explanation: Meningiomas arise from arachnoid cap cells and form extra-axial masses with whorled architecture and frequently laminated calcifications (psammoma bodies).
Source Section: Adult Primary Brain Tumors; PDF pp. 152
Notes: Psammoma bodies may be absent and are not unique to meningioma (also papillary thyroid Ca, serous ovarian Ca); these are characteristic combined clues. Dural tail is a related imaging sign.

Explanation: Primary CNS lymphoma is usually a CD20-positive B-cell lymphoma (commonly DLBCL); its immunodeficiency-associated form is strongly linked to EBV.
Source Section: Adult Primary Brain Tumors; PDF pp. 153
Notes: EBV association is strongest in immunodeficiency-associated disease; do not generalize to immunocompetent PCNSL, where EBV is usually negative. Title scoped accordingly.

Explanation: Ischemic brain injury may result from local large-vessel thrombosis, embolic obstruction, small penetrating-vessel disease, or global systemic hypoperfusion (watershed).
Notes: These are mechanisms, which are not always mutually exclusive etiologic categories (cf. TOAST classification). Clean board-relevant set.

Explanation: Branches of the MCA perfuse lateral frontal, temporal, and parietal regions involved in language and face/arm motor control.
Notes: Several other MCA-supplied regions also qualify; this is a source-grounded subset. Do not imply a single MCA branch supplies all four or that every MCA stroke involves all. Leg-predominant motor cortex is ACA, not MCA.

Explanation: Lateral medullary injury (PICA/vertebral) affects the nucleus ambiguus, spinal trigeminal nucleus/tract, spinothalamic tract, and descending sympathetic fibers.
Notes: Use the full pattern for localization. Sensory and sympathetic signs overlap lateral pontine syndrome; nucleus ambiguus involvement (hoarseness/dysphagia) favors the medullary site. Overlaps NEU-007.

Explanation: A traumatic epidural hematoma classically involves middle meningeal arterial bleeding outside the dura with a biconvex CT collection that does not cross suture lines; some patients have a transient lucid interval.
Source Section: Aneurysms and Intracranial Hemorrhage; PDF pp. 171
Notes: Not every epidural bleed is arterial (venous EDH occurs) or has a lucid interval; 'possible' wording preserved. Pairs as a contrast set with NEU-039 (subdural).

Explanation: Bridging-vein injury produces a crescentic subdural collection that can cross suture lines; cerebral atrophy (elderly, alcohol use) increases susceptibility.
Source Section: Aneurysms and Intracranial Hemorrhage; PDF pp. 171
Notes: Older age/atrophy is a risk factor, not a diagnostic requirement; infants (shaken) and anticoagulated patients are also at risk. Contrast set with NEU-038.

Tile 3: Blood in basal cisterns on CT
Explanation: Blood in the subarachnoid space (often ruptured aneurysm) causes abrupt severe headache and meningeal irritation and may be seen in the basal cisterns on CT or detected as CSF xanthochromia.
Source Section: Aneurysms and Intracranial Hemorrhage; PDF pp. 171, 173
Notes: Xanthochromia depends on timing (develops ~6-12 h) and spectrophotometric testing. These are associations, not a mandate to perform LP in every case.

Explanation: Cerebellar dysfunction impairs movement accuracy (dysmetria), rapid alternating movement (dysdiadochokinesia), target-directed movement (intention tremor), and axial balance (truncal ataxia).
Source Section: Ischemic Cerebrovascular Accidents; Cerebellum and Ventricles; PDF pp. 162, 181
Notes: Truncal ataxia favors vermis/midline; limb signs favor the ipsilateral cerebellar hemisphere. One focal lesion need not produce all four.

Explanation: ATM-mutation disease (autosomal recessive) combines progressive cerebellar ataxia, telangiectasias, and immunodeficiency that can include IgA deficiency and increased malignancy risk.
Notes: IgA deficiency is a common but variable feature, not a universal diagnostic criterion. Elevated AFP and radiosensitivity are related clues.

Connection Title: Friedreich ataxia genetic and systemic clues
Explanation: Friedreich ataxia links an intronic GAA repeat expansion in the frataxin (FXN) gene and reduced frataxin to neurologic disease with possible hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and diabetes.
Notes: Cardiomyopathy and diabetes are frequent but not universal (more common with earlier onset/larger expansions). 'Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy' kept generic (not all obstructive). Verified: Parkinson et al., J Neurochem 2013.

Explanation: Hypothalamic circuits integrate feeding, thermoregulation, circadian timing (suprachiasmatic nucleus), and neuroendocrine control of growth (via GHRH/somatostatin).
Notes: Integrative category, broader than disease-mechanism groups. Tile 4 is hypothalamic regulation of growth (GHRH/somatostatin), NOT direct GH secretion (that is anterior pituitary); wording reflects this.

Explanation: Congenital GnRH deficiency with failed GnRH-neuron/olfactory migration produces anosmia and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with delayed or absent puberty.
Notes: Not all congenital GnRH deficiency is Kallmann (Kallmann = with anosmia). Clean developmental set.

Explanation: A pineal-region or dorsal midbrain lesion disrupts pretectal eye-movement circuitry (posterior commissure, riMLF) and can obstruct the cerebral aqueduct, causing hydrocephalus.
Notes: Aqueductal obstruction is a frequent cause/consequence of the mass, not an eye sign; elevated CSF pressure/hydrocephalus itself can produce Parinaud. Collier lid retraction is a related sign. Verified: Weidauer et al., Neuroradiology 2019; Abid et al., Neurology 2016; Frank et al., Neurology 2022.

Connection Title: Wilson disease neurologic and systemic clues
Explanation: Wilson disease (ATP7B, impaired copper excretion) combines hepatic disease, movement disorder (including wing-beating tremor), neuropsychiatric change, and corneal copper (Kayser-Fleischer rings).
Notes: Manifestations vary by stage; not every patient has all four (hepatic presentations may precede KF rings/neuro signs). Low ceruloplasmin and high urinary copper are related labs.

Explanation: These four classic dopamine circuits underlie reward/positive psychotic symptoms, cortical/negative symptoms, movement, and prolactin inhibition respectively.
Source Section: Neurotransmitter Activity in Psychiatric Disease; PDF pp. 200
Notes: Identifies circuits, not a claim that psychiatric disease is a single transmitter imbalance. Antipsychotic effects (nigrostriatal EPS, tuberoinfundibular hyperprolactinemia) are the board-relevant payoff.

Explanation: Alzheimer pathology features extracellular amyloid-beta plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles made of hyperphosphorylated tau; vascular amyloid deposition (CAA) commonly coexists.
Notes: PARTIAL REDUNDANCY: hyperphosphorylated tau is the constituent protein of neurofibrillary tangles, so tiles 2 and 3 are closely linked (structure vs molecule) - retain as distinct teaching points but flag redundancy on a board. CAA can also occur independently. Verified: Kim et al., J Alzheimers Dis 2026; Barthelemy et al., Nat Med 2020.

Explanation: Three cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) and an NMDA-receptor antagonist (memantine) are used for symptomatic treatment of Alzheimer dementia.
Notes: This is an INDICATION category, not a shared-mechanism group: memantine (NMDA antagonist) differs mechanistically and is used in moderate-severe disease. Does not imply these are the complete modern options (anti-amyloid mAbs now exist). BOARD OVERLAP: donepezil/rivastigmine/galantamine also appear in NEU-015.

Explanation: Parkinson disease presents with bradykinesia, a 4-6 Hz resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity, and (typically later) postural instability.
Notes: Resting tremor may be absent (akinetic-rigid variant); postural instability is usually later. Very early falls/instability suggest atypical parkinsonism (e.g., PSP).

Explanation: These therapies increase dopaminergic activity by precursor replacement (levodopa), receptor agonism, or reduced dopamine/levodopa metabolism (COMT and MAO-B inhibition).
Notes: Mixed single-drug and drug-class tiles. COMT inhibitors (e.g., entacapone) are levodopa adjuncts, not stand-alone substitutes. Anticholinergics/amantadine are other classes not included.

Explanation: DLB presents with fluctuating cognition, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism, and marked sensitivity to antipsychotics; REM sleep behavior disorder is also supportive.
Notes: Neuroleptic sensitivity is a supportive feature; the three core features are fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, and parkinsonism (plus RBD). Do not label all four as formal core criteria.

Explanation: Prion disease (sporadic CJD) causes rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, cortical spongiform change, and periodic sharp-wave EEG complexes in appropriate subtypes.
Notes: Periodic sharp waves are neither universal nor specific to all prion diseases (less common in variant CJD). RT-QuIC and CSF 14-3-3/MRI DWI are modern supportive tests not captured here.

Connection Title: Potentially treatable contributors to cognitive impairment
Explanation: These are potentially treatable conditions that can contribute to or mimic a dementia presentation and should be screened for in cognitive decline.
Notes: Depression-related cognitive impairment is a reversible mimic; established neurologic injury from B12 deficiency or neurosyphilis may not fully reverse. Avoid the blanket label 'fully reversible dementias.'

Explanation: Migraine commonly combines moderate-severe pulsatile, often unilateral pain with photophobia/phonophobia and nausea/vomiting, worsened by activity.
Notes: Migraine may be bilateral, and not every attack has all four. Similar features can occur in secondary headaches; red-flag screening (SNNOOP10) is needed before labeling migraine.

Connection Title: Cluster headache ipsilateral cranial autonomic signs
Explanation: Cluster headache activates ipsilateral cranial autonomic/trigeminal-autonomic pathways, producing tearing, rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, and a partial Horner (miosis/ptosis).
Notes: These autonomic features are shared by all trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias (paroxysmal hemicrania, SUNCT), so they are not cluster-specific; avoid a competing TAC category on the same board. Attack duration/frequency distinguishes the TACs.

Explanation: IIH (typically young obese women) causes papilledema, pulsatile tinnitus, a false-localizing CN VI palsy, and raised LP opening pressure with normal CSF constituents and neuroimaging.
Notes: Secondary intracranial hypertension (venous sinus thrombosis, drugs) can mimic all four; IIH is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring normal imaging/CSF. Raised pressure alone is not diagnostic.

Explanation: Typical childhood absence seizures cause brief awareness lapses with immediate recovery and a 3-Hz generalized spike-and-wave EEG; ethosuximide is first-line for absence-only epilepsy.
Notes: Ethosuximide does not cover coexisting generalized tonic-clonic seizures (use valproate/lamotrigine then). Hyperventilation provocation is a related clue.

Explanation: These are classic generalized-onset seizure forms distinguished by awareness change and motor pattern.
Notes: Title specifies generalized-ONSET: under the current ILAE 2017 classification, tonic-clonic, myoclonic, and atonic events can also occur with focal or unknown onset. Framing as generalized-onset avoids inaccuracy.

Explanation: Rotational acceleration-deceleration forces shear axons, characteristically at the gray-white junction and corpus callosum, producing axonal retraction bulbs.
Notes: Mixed tile types (two locations, a histologic finding, a mechanism) are acceptable for this clue category. CT may be normal; MRI (SWI/GRE) is more sensitive, and microhemorrhage is not universal.
